testcase: Are cost management capabilities available in Azure MCP Server?
query:
title: Are cost management capabilities available in Azure MCP Server?

question: My customer needs cost analysis capabilities in Azure MCP Server. I found a closed PR for a CostManagement query tool. Are cost management tools available today, and is there a roadmap for exposing them through Azure MCP Server?
ground_truth:
A number of cost management operation tools are available today in the ARM MCP Server, but they are currently behind a custom header. Azure MCP Server proxies into ARM MCP Server, but these tools are not exposed through Azure MCP Server yet because of the custom-header requirement.

The Azure MCP Server team and the ARM MCP team are actively working on exposing those cost management capabilities through Azure MCP Server. In the meantime, historical cost queries can be done through the Azure Skills plugin, and additional cost-related workflows are being explored.

For more information, see [Introducing Cost Management and Pricing Toolsets in Azure Resource Manager MCP Server](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/FinOpsBlog/introducing-cost-management-and-pricing-toolsets-in-azure-resource-manager-mcp-s/4530710) and the [Azure cost skills](https://github.com/microsoft/azure-skills/tree/main/skills/azure-cost).

expected_references.title: Introducing Cost Management and Pricing Toolsets in Azure Resource Manager MCP Server

testcase: Do I need a first-party app registration to deploy remote Azure MCP Server with OBO?
query:
title: Do I need a first-party app registration to deploy remote Azure MCP Server with OBO?

question: I want to integrate Azure MCP Server with an agent client in an Azure production service. The documented DIY remote deployment uses on-behalf-of authentication. Do I need a first-party Microsoft Entra app registration that can request ARM tokens OBO, or can this be done with another type of app registration? Is there a managed remote Azure MCP Server offering?
ground_truth:
You do not need a first-party app registration to provision remote Azure MCP Server with on-behalf-of authentication. You need a Microsoft Entra ID app registration, and that app registration can be third-party.

For a managed offering, the Azure MCP team is working with the connector namespaces team on a managed solution, but there is not a committed release date yet. If the scenario is for an Azure production service or production AI agent that serves Azure customers across tenants, the technical requirements are different from a team-internal use case, so the Azure MCP team will want to understand the client, expected call volume, user volume, and tenant requirements before giving detailed guidance.

See [Deploy the Azure MCP Server with On-Behalf-Of Authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/developer/azure-mcp-server/how-to/deploy-remote-mcp-server-on-behalf-of?tabs=csharp).

expected_references.title: Deploy the Azure MCP Server with On-Behalf-Of Authentication

testcase: Should Azure MCP tools embed thousands of metadata files as resources?
query:
title: Should Azure MCP tools embed thousands of metadata files as resources?

question: We are building an Azure MCP tool that depends on many metadata files, such as PowerShell and JSON files. The data is not exposed in Azure Resource Graph or ARM APIs, so we are considering checking the files into the Azure MCP tool repository. The files are individually small, but there may be thousands of them, starting around 100 files and 2 MB and potentially growing to tens of MB. Is there guidance or a hard cap for embedding these resources, and what approach is recommended?
ground_truth:
Avoid embedding a large and growing metadata corpus directly into the Azure MCP tool assembly. Embedded resources across all tools are currently small, around 0.8 MB total, so a single area adding 2 MB and later tens of MB would noticeably increase the Azure MCP binary size.

The recommended approach is to follow the pattern used by the AzureTerraform tool's AzApiExampleService:

- Host the metadata in a separate repository or Azure Blob Storage, versioned independently from Azure MCP releases.
- Have the tool fetch a small index or manifest for the relevant subset based on input parameters.
- Pull only the matching files on demand instead of downloading or embedding the entire dataset.

This keeps the Azure MCP binary size flat as the dataset grows and allows metadata updates to ship without requiring an Azure MCP release.

testcase: What should I do if Azure MCP Server fails from an Azure Dev Box?
query:
title: What should I do if Azure MCP Server fails from an Azure Dev Box?

question: Connections from an Azure Dev Box to Azure MCP Server are failing. Is Azure MCP Server down, and what should I try first?
ground_truth:
Azure MCP Server is not necessarily down when this happens. A likely cause is an `npx` cache issue on the machine.

Run the following command first to warm up the `npx` cache and download the Azure MCP binary before using the server:

```bash
npx @azure/mcp --version
```

After the binary has been downloaded and cached, retry the Azure MCP Server connection.

testcase: Is the Azure MCP Application Insights connection string embedded by design?
query:
title: Is the Azure MCP Application Insights connection string embedded by design?

question: Azure MCP Server appears to hardcode an Application Insights connection string in `OpenTelemetryExtensions.cs` for release builds, with telemetry opt-out controlled by `AZURE_MCP_COLLECT_TELEMETRY_MICROSOFT=false`. Since the ingestion key is visible in source, is embedding the connection string by design, and what mitigations are in place against forged or noisy telemetry?
ground_truth:
Yes, the Application Insights connection string is embedded by design. The Application Insights instrumentation key is not considered a secret; it is more of an identifier. The Azure Monitor documentation also notes that connection strings and instrumentation keys are not secrets.

Azure MCP telemetry is filtered through the DevDiv telemetry DataX platform before the team processes it. Properties that are not part of the known telemetry schema are dropped, which helps prevent unexpected data from polluting the processed telemetry. The team considered keeping the connection string out of source, but that would require users to authenticate before publishing telemetry, which would add other complications.

Independent skill or plugin repositories should not use the Azure MCP Server's App Insights key. Those repositories are under their own ownership and need to work with their privacy team to determine data handling requirements, including what telemetry can be collected and where it can be persisted. If App Insights is appropriate for an independent system, teams can use their own telemetry setup, such as a DataX-backed path or Log Analytics, depending on compliance requirements.

See [Azure Monitor connection strings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/app/connection-strings).

testcase: How should a service team onboard many tools to Azure MCP Server?
query:
title: How should a service team onboard many tools to Azure MCP Server?

question: I created an onboarding issue for adding a new service toolset to Azure MCP Server. The proposed toolset maps directly to service operations and includes about 75 tools. Before submitting the first PR, should I do anything else, and can all tools be added up front?
ground_truth:
Before submitting the first PR, the Azure MCP team will assign an onboarding buddy. The onboarding buddy will work with the service team to review the tool proposal, consolidate the design, and provide feedback on PRs.

The guidance is to start with high-value scenarios instead of adding every service operation up front. Tool sprawl is a quality risk for agents and user experiences because too many tools increase decision load and tool-selection churn, causing more retries and slower, less accurate execution.

A better onboarding path is:

- Identify the highest-value service scenarios, using telemetry or usage data from the service SDK where available.
- Start with a small set of hero scenarios rather than full operation coverage.
- Consolidate similar operations where possible, such as using a single list tool for related resource types when the design supports it.
- Submit small PRs, ideally around 4 to 5 tools per PR, to make review easier and enable phased rollout.
- Expand over time based on real user behavior and high-usage scenarios.

There is no strict required time gap between tool drops. The cadence is driven more by user behavior and scenario value than by a fixed schedule.

testcase: How should an OAuth-protected registry MCP server be added to Azure MCP?
query:
title: How should an OAuth-protected registry MCP server be added to Azure MCP?

question: I want to add an OAuth-protected registry MCP server to the official Microsoft MCP server list and potentially make it available through Azure MCP. What needs to happen before it can be merged, and what authentication scenarios should be tested?
ground_truth:
Adding a Microsoft MCP server to the official list and integrating it into Azure MCP should be treated as separate conversations. The first step can be a PR that adds the MCP server to the official Microsoft MCP server list. A separate onboarding discussion is needed to decide whether and how it should be exposed through Azure MCP.

Before Azure MCP integration, open an onboarding request that explains what features the server brings to Azure MCP users and summarizes the tools it adds. The project lead needs to sign off before the Azure MCP integration can merge, and an onboarding buddy can help with the code changes and review process.

Because the registry MCP server uses OAuth, the team should test and document a matrix of supported and unsupported authentication scenarios:

- Azure MCP stdio plus user principal, such as accessing the registry server from Azure MCP in stdio mode with Azure CLI credential.
- Azure MCP stdio plus service principal, such as accessing the registry server from Azure MCP in stdio mode with managed identity credential.
- Azure MCP remote plus user principal OBO, where the client passes a user principal token to Azure MCP in remote mode.
- Azure MCP remote plus service principal OBO, where the client passes a service principal token to Azure MCP in remote mode.

If the PR is only for listing the server as an official Microsoft MCP server and not for exposing it through Azure MCP, keep the PR scoped to the official list and avoid unrelated Azure MCP registry changes.

testcase: How can a partner team get access to the Azure Skills telemetry Power BI dashboard?
query:
title: How can a partner team get access to the Azure Skills telemetry Power BI dashboard?

question: A partner team owns an Azure Skill and wants access to the telemetry dashboard for that skill. The onboarding documentation explains how to request access to the Kusto cluster for telemetry data, but how should they get access to the Power BI dashboard?
ground_truth:
Access to the Azure Skills telemetry Power BI dashboard is granted through security group membership. The partner team should follow the onboarding instructions, which include joining the required security groups.

For the Power BI dashboard specifically, joining the `azmcppartners` security group automatically grants access to the dashboard.

Relevant links are also available from the Microsoft employee instructions and from the `CONTRIBUTING.md` file in the open-source repository.

testcase: How do I get access to run the ToolDescriptionEvaluator?
query:
title: How do I get access to run the ToolDescriptionEvaluator?

question: I want to run the `ToolDescriptionEvaluator`, but I do not have the API key for the Azure OpenAI endpoint used by the tool. How can I get access, and how should I run the evaluator efficiently?
ground_truth:
To get access to the test Azure OpenAI account used by `ToolDescriptionEvaluator`, first get access to the Azure tenant where the Azure MCP test resources are hosted. The team refers to this tenant as TME. Follow point 4 in the Getting Started section of the Azure MCP getting-started documentation. Access to that document requires VPN or corpnet.

After submitting the tenant access request, your manager needs to approve it. Once approved, you should be able to access the test Azure OpenAI resource and retrieve the endpoint and credentials.

For running the evaluator, use the [ToolDescriptionEvaluator quickstart guide](https://github.com/microsoft/mcp/blob/main/eng/tools/ToolDescriptionEvaluator/Quickstart.md). Run it with an area filter for the tools you added, for example:

```bash
dotnet run -- --area "keyvault"
```

Avoid running without a filter unless you intend to evaluate all tools. Running against every tool usually takes more than 10 minutes, while an area-filtered run usually completes in a few seconds.

testcase: What telemetry dimensions and exports are supported for Azure MCP tools and skills?
query:
title: What telemetry dimensions and exports are supported for Azure MCP tools and skills?

question: For Azure MCP telemetry, are there plans to support tool calls or skills invoked by model type, MAU/MEU/MDU for individual tools, and ranked lists of tool calls by tool? Also, should users be able to export dashboard data to Excel?
ground_truth:
The Power BI report can support additional dimensions if the underlying telemetry has that dimension. If `model type` is available in the telemetry data, the team can update the LENS job that cooks the data for the report, and the report will load the updated data on its next refresh schedule. For calls made from VS Code, model type should be correlatable because VS Code telemetry tracks which model processed a prompt. Outside VS Code, model type is generally not available to the MCP server, so it is not generally possible to correlate.

Daily active users can already be filtered by available dimensions. However, MAU/MEU/MDU for one specific MCP tool is not always a meaningful product concept, because users are not expected to invoke a single MCP tool daily in the same way they might use VS Code or Teams daily. If a team still needs that analysis, they can query the data directly in Kusto or use [Kusto Workbench](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=angelos-petropoulos.vscode-kusto-workbench), which can create charts and publish Power BI reports.

For ranked tool-call analysis, use Kusto or Kusto Workbench against the available telemetry fields, and create charts or publish a custom Power BI report if needed. Exporting Power BI data to Excel may be disabled because MSIT does not prefer reports being exported and shared through file types that cannot protect and audit the access trail.

testcase: Can Copilot CLI installs and Azure Skills usage be tracked for an event or lab?
query:
title: Can Copilot CLI installs and Azure Skills usage be tracked for an event or lab?

question: We are using Copilot CLI as a key surface for a lab and want to understand installs and usage during the event. Can we track Azure plugin installs, usage of the `microsoft-foundry` skill, and sub-skill activity within that skill from telemetry?
ground_truth:
There is not a direct metric for Azure plugin installs from Copilot CLI. As a proxy, you can use `devdeviceId` counts to see whether usage increases for a particular skill such as `microsoft-foundry`. `devdeviceId` is unique per user across clients, so adding a client-name filter such as Copilot CLI can help approximate the metric.

The Azure Skills telemetry dashboard can show per-file or sub-skill access counts, which can provide useful coarse-grained tracking for a specific skill. Teams can use the Azure Skills reference files Power BI dashboard and add a Foundry-specific view if that helps their analysis.

When interpreting client filters, `copilot-cli` covers metrics from GitHub Copilot CLI, including the Copilot CLI terminal in VS Code. `Visual Studio Code` covers metrics from GitHub Copilot Chat in VS Code.

testcase: Where should I look when the Microsoft Foundry deploy skill fails for hosted agents?
query:
title: Where should I look when the Microsoft Foundry deploy skill fails for hosted agents?

question: I am using Azure Skills for a Build lab. The `observe` skill works with a prompt agent endpoint, and I can use the `create` skill to create and locally test a hosted agent. However, the `deploy` skill fails. Are the create and deploy skills updated for the new hosted agents runtime, and where should I look first to troubleshoot?
ground_truth:
The Foundry Skills contributors can help troubleshoot hosted-agent create and deploy issues. The skills have been updated toward ADC-based hosted agents, so if create works but deploy fails, a likely first thing to check is region availability.

Make sure the currently logged-in Azure subscription has access to create projects in a region supported by hosted agents. Then retry create and deploy in a supported region.

See the hosted agents region availability documentation: [Hosted agents region availability](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/hosted-agents#region-availability).

testcase: How does Azure MCP Server authenticate in local and remote transport modes?
query:
title: How does Azure MCP Server authenticate in local and remote transport modes?

question: Azure MCP Server can run locally with stdio transport or remotely with HTTP transport. How does authentication differ between these two modes, and what should I configure for local development, CI/CD, or production hosting?
ground_truth:
Azure MCP Server uses different authentication models depending on the transport mode.

In local stdio mode, inbound authentication is not required because communication happens over local process pipes. The server itself authenticates to Azure using credentials available on the developer machine. It uses a chained credential flow and selects the first credential that succeeds. The chain can include environment credentials, Visual Studio, Visual Studio Code, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, Azure Developer CLI, and interactive browser credentials. In VS Code, running `Azure: Sign In` from the Command Palette is a quick way to authenticate.

You can pin a specific credential by setting `AZURE_TOKEN_CREDENTIALS` to the credential name. For example, to use only Azure CLI authentication, set `AZURE_TOKEN_CREDENTIALS=AzureCliCredential`. You can also set `AZURE_MCP_ONLY_USE_BROKER_CREDENTIAL=true` to use the OS authentication broker, such as Web Account Manager on Windows, with browser login fallback on unsupported operating systems.

In remote HTTP mode, every inbound request must be protected with Microsoft Entra ID bearer tokens. The outbound authentication model depends on the configured outgoing authentication strategy.

Recommended setup by environment:

- For local development, sign in with `az login`, the VS Code Azure extension, or Azure PowerShell and let the credential chain pick up the login.
- For CI/CD pipelines, set `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`, and `AZURE_TENANT_ID` for service principal authentication.
- For production hosting, HTTP transport is recommended. If stdio is required in production, set `AZURE_TOKEN_CREDENTIALS=prod` to restrict credentials to non-interactive production-safe credentials such as environment, workload identity, and managed identity.

Regardless of the credential source, the authenticated identity must have the required Azure RBAC roles on the target resources. For user-assigned managed identity, also set `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` to the managed identity client ID; otherwise, system-assigned managed identity is used.

testcase: How do I connect Azure MCP Server to Azure sovereign clouds?
query:
title: How do I connect Azure MCP Server to Azure sovereign clouds?

question: By default Azure MCP Server authenticates against Azure Public Cloud. How can I configure it to connect to Azure China Cloud or Azure US Government, and what should I check if authentication fails?
ground_truth:
Azure MCP Server supports sovereign clouds by configuring the cloud environment used for authentication. By default it uses Azure Public Cloud through `login.microsoftonline.com`. To use a sovereign cloud, specify a supported well-known cloud name. URL-like values and custom authority hosts are not accepted.

Supported cloud names include:

- Azure Public Cloud: `AzureCloud`, `AzurePublicCloud`, `Public`, or `AzurePublic`
- Azure China Cloud: `AzureChinaCloud`, `China`, or `AzureChina`
- Azure US Government: `AzureUSGovernment`, `USGov`, `AzureUSGovernmentCloud`, or `USGovernment`

The aliases are case insensitive.

The highest-priority configuration method is the `--cloud` command-line option:

```bash
azmcp server start --cloud AzureChinaCloud
azmcp server start --cloud AzureUSGovernment
```

You can also configure the cloud through configuration keys such as `AZURE_CLOUD`, `azure_cloud`, `cloud`, or `Cloud`, or by setting the `AZURE_CLOUD` environment variable. If no cloud is configured, Azure MCP Server falls back to `AzurePublicCloud`.

Before connecting to a sovereign cloud, authenticate local tools against the same cloud. For example, with Azure CLI:

```bash
az cloud set --name AzureChinaCloud
az login
azmcp server start --cloud AzureChinaCloud
```

If authentication fails, verify that the cloud configuration is correct, that local tools are authenticated against the same cloud, that the tenant ID belongs to the target cloud, and that the authority host is reachable from the network. Verbose or debug logging can help confirm which authority host is being used.

testcase: How should I handle the VS Code 128-tool limit with Azure MCP Server?
query:
title: How should I handle the VS Code 128-tool limit with Azure MCP Server?

question: When I configure Azure MCP Server together with other comprehensive MCP servers, VS Code Copilot reports that I may not include more than 128 tools in a request. Why does this happen, and what are the recommended workarounds?
ground_truth:
This happens because VS Code Copilot has a 128-tool limit per request. If you load Azure MCP with all tools and combine it with other broad toolsets, such as a GitHub MCP server configured with all tools, the combined tool count can exceed the limit.

The recommended approaches are:

- Use VS Code custom chat modes for scenario-specific tool configurations. Create different modes for different workflows and keep each mode under the 128-tool limit.
- Use selective tool loading with `--namespace` to expose only tools for specific Azure services, such as `storage` or `keyvault`.
- Use `--tool` to expose only specific tool names when you need very granular control.
- Use consolidated mode with `azmcp server start --mode consolidated`. This groups related operations into curated tools, keeps the tool count well below the limit, and is optimized for AI agents.
- Use single tool proxy mode with `azmcp server start --mode single` when you want Azure MCP to expose one tool that internally routes to Azure services.

For example, instead of loading every Azure MCP tool, you can start only Storage and Key Vault namespaces:

```bash
npx -y @azure/mcp@latest server start --namespace storage --namespace keyvault
```

To check the current tool count in VS Code, open the Command Palette, run `MCP: List Servers`, and inspect the tool count for each configured server.
